answer_text:
# 💜 The History of Purple

---

## In the Beginning: A Rare Colour in a Raw World

If we go back to our prehistoric existence, our ancestors probably never saw a purple fruit, flower, bird, fish — or any living thing — because purple is very rare in nature. Yet even in that ancient world, the urge to make colour was irresistible. Purple is said to have first appeared in art during the Neolithic era. Prehistoric artists in France used sticks of manganese and hematite powder to draw and paint animals and outlines on the walls of their caves — works dated back to between 16,000 and 25,000 BC.

These early smears of violet pigment were accidental, primitive — nothing like the rich, blazing purple that would one day crown emperors and alter the fate of chemistry. That story begins by the sea.

---

## The Snail and the Sea: Tyrian Purple

The story goes back around 3,000 years to the Phoenicians, a seafaring civilization living along the Mediterranean coast — in modern Lebanon, Syria, and Israel. Purple was first sourced in Phoenicia — a name that itself translates as *"purple land."*

The dye stemmed from the foul-smelling mucous gland of a marine mollusc. As a result, the very word *purple* owes itself to the Latin word for a purple shellfish: *purpura.* The first shade produced was Tyrian purple, created from *Bolinus brandaris* sea snails. Dye makers harvested mucus from the shell, heated it in an alkaline solution, dipped yarn into it, and exposed it to sunlight — turning it purple.

The process was backbreaking, and the smell was notoriously unbearable. It took some 12,000 shellfish to extract just 1.5 grams of the pure dye — barely enough to colour a single garment the size of a Roman toga. The unique thing about Tyrian purple was its ability to retain its colour over time, even becoming brighter with age rather than fading. For an ancient world where most colours bled and faded in sunlight, this was extraordinary — almost supernatural.

---

## The Colour of Gods and Emperors

Tyrian purple was associated with the rank of royalty in the ancient civilisations of Rome, Japan, Persia, Egypt, and Constantinople, dating back as far as the 16th century BC.

Deemed decadent and valuable, purple was reserved only for the elite — rulers, high-ranking religious clergy, and those of royal rank. In Ancient Greece, legislation stated that the higher your status, the more right you had to wear purple. In Rome, purple had connections with Julius Caesar, who famously sported a purple toga, while wealthy men of a noble class known as the *equites* were permitted to wear robes with a Tyrian Purple stripe.

As the Roman Empire deepened its grip, so too did its grip on purple. Roman emperors passed "sumptuary laws" to control who could wear it. Only the emperor could wear a robe fully dyed in purple. Senators could wear a white toga with a single purple stripe. Priests used purple garments during sacred rituals. Emperor Nero famously forbade anyone other than the emperor from wearing the colour, under penalty of death.

In Byzantine times — 330 AD to 1453 AD — purple was even more strongly associated with royalty and high-ranking clergy. The term *"born to the purple"* referred to Byzantine emperors born during the reign of their fathers, meaning they were legitimate heirs.

---

## The Middle Ages: Purple and the Church

As the Roman Empire crumbled, purple did not disappear — it was absorbed by the Church. Purple was worn by the upper class, and artists commissioned by the Catholic Church also depicted Jesus and the Virgin Mary in purple. Once the colour of Caesar's and Catholic cardinals' robes, purple was long associated with royalty and being *"born to the purple."*

But the supply of Tyrian purple was finite. Making the dye was painstaking and stinky work that virtually drove the gastropods to extinction — hence the eventual change to red robes for cardinals.

The Byzantine Empire, which had controlled the dye trade, declined. The technique of making the dye was kept secret, passed down within families, and eventually lost. Cheaper dyes made from plants became more practical. By the time of the Renaissance, the original recipe for Tyrian purple was forgotten. People knew it had once existed, but nobody knew how to make it anymore.

Yet its legend endured. During the Elizabethan era, purple was reserved for royalty, and throughout England's Tudor period only King Henry VIII was allowed to dress in the colour — he went as far as committing an Earl to death by treason for wearing it.

---

## The Accident That Changed Everything: Mauve, 1856

Then came a teenager, a laboratory, and a spectacular mistake.

In 1856, an 18-year-old English chemist, William Henry Perkin, mistakenly invented *Perkin's Purple* — the shade we recognise today as mauveine or mauve. He was at the time trying to find a cure for malaria by attempting to synthesise quinine in a laboratory. When cleaning up the solution he'd created with alcohol, he noticed he'd produced a dark purple liquid.

In the lab he'd set up in his parents' loft, he stained a piece of cloth in the brilliant purple solution — and he couldn't remove it by washing. He realised this colour, which *"resisted the action of the atmosphere, light, and soap,"* had tremendous potential.

He initially labelled it *Tyrian purple*, to capitalise on history, but soon switched to calling it *mauve*, after the French name for the mallow flower. The vibrant mauveine purple was derived from coal tar and made its creator a Fellow of the Royal Society and Royal Medallist.

His purple dyestuff marked the beginning of a revolution in organic chemistry — the birth of an industry that has since given us a rainbow of colours, as well as drugs, explosives, fertilisers, plastics, and synthetics beyond measure. For the first time in history, purple was no longer the preserve of emperors and popes. It was available to anyone who could afford a yard of fashionable fabric.

---

## Purple Across Cultures

Even as it democratised, purple never shed its aura of significance. Different cultures coloured it with their own meanings. Japan sees purple as a symbol of nobility and strength, which can be traced back to the Heian period when purple was associated with the imperial family. Thailand, however, views purple as sombre — widows often wear it during periods of mourning. India ties purple to spirituality and peace, frequently using it during religious ceremonies.
